is_kelvins_design:
A reduced variant of FRAME section 5, not the full design.
Kept: the score reads only the finished demonstration; the target is in proportion to the score; the writer's internals are not submitted; the trust head is fitted on real answers only.
Drifts:
1. The simple world model is its own exact sampler. T is M's own left-to-right writing law, and one line carries 0.77-0.85 of the whole score, so no search is ever needed to find the high-scoring demonstration.
2. The rollout policy is not a GFlowNet and is not trained toward the score. The writers are LoRAs tuned by supervised learning on hand-built text. There are no alien states (the writer writes the demonstration itself) and no distillation.
3. The amplification is three fixed hand-written rules. Nothing is learned and rollouts do not read each other.
4. The trust head reads one number.
5. Section 6 says consistency is about query orders. The note files writer-independence under his consistency requirement (Q6 b); it is policy independence. Query-order consistency is untested.
6. The score has no goal or reality-trained factor beyond a format regex.
Written by hand: both task families and the line format; the regex; M's prompt with four generator-solved examples; the three aggregation rules; the biased writers' errors (built from exact answers); the trust head's input; the certificate threshold 1/2.

verdicts.claim: Registered bin is MINOR, not MAJOR (H4 missed for W3 on variables by 0.008).
verdicts.reason: My own code (check/code/recheck.py) on the stored rollouts reproduces every threshold number. PREREG was hashed 16:59:07Z; the test run was 17:15:52-18:10:27Z (cluster file times). Fresh data (32 new problems per family, job 57920, my sampler and scorer, float32): H1, H2, H3 hold; H4 misses again for W3 on variables, by more (0.110 against bar 0.082). So MINOR is not a near-MAJOR. Gap: analyze.py was edited after the hash and the original was not kept.

verdicts.claim: Plain vote follows the biased writer W3 (0.567 / 0.353 against 0.987 / 0.920; distance 0.43-0.54 up to K=256).
verdicts.reason: Stored: identical. Fresh: 0.531 / 0.406 against 0.969 / 0.812; distance 0.44 / 0.56, flat in K. A second tuning seed (W3r) gives 0.594 / 0.344.

verdicts.claim: For the three biased writers built, score-based aggregations keep accuracy within 0.03 of M's own vote, excess movement <= 0.024.
verdicts.reason: Stored: identical. Fresh: (b) equals or beats M's own vote for all three and for W3r; (c) is one problem below the bar for W3s and W3p on variables (0.781 against 0.812, n=32); excess movement up to 0.067. But this is close to true by construction: each of the three writers writes M's single top line in 34-71% of its rollouts (W3 was tuned on one M rollout per problem), so that line is missing from 16 rollouts in at most 5% of cases.

verdicts.claim: The helpful writer W4 moves every aggregation 0.13-0.15 from the target on variables at every K; found score 0.69 against 0.86.
verdicts.reason: Stored: identical, including K=256. Fresh: 0.21-0.23 at every K, found score 0.60 against 0.88. The size is arithmetic, not a property of the aggregations: W4 writes one line, so the distance is 1 minus the target's probability of the right answer.

verdicts.claim: Three registered expectations were wrong (dedup-score would not return; trust head would improve W1's Brier; E1 for W3).
verdicts.reason: Recomputed: dedup from W1 0.048 / 0.041 against bar 0.077; my trust fit 0.036 -> 0.037; W3 importance-weighted 0.077 against 0.074 at K=256 on variables.

verdicts.claim: Interval from the score alone, valid for any writer; found score > 1/2 certifies the target's majority answer.
verdicts.reason: Re-derived. Fresh, float32: no violation beyond the reference's noise (max 0.013); the certified answer is the reference's top answer in every cell, the two new writers included. Scope the note does not state: the proof needs the total score to be at most 1, true only because the score is M's own probability. A general score has no known total, so no share found. The table is post hoc, as said.

verdicts.claim: A trust head on the vote breaks when the writer is swapped (0.037 -> 0.345) and carries over on score-based aggregations for the three biased writers.
verdicts.reason: My fit on stored data: identical. 'Breaks' is W3 only: W3s and W3p degrade by 0.020 and 0.035, below the registered 0.05. Fresh: vote 0.082 -> 0.330; on (b) within 0.02 for the three. It does not carry over to a writer that never writes M's lines: on (b), Brier 0.92 for my W5 (stated confidence 0.99, right 5%).

verdicts.claim: The target is M's belief after thinking, not truth: top answer wrong on 8% of variable problems, reproduced by score-based aggregation.
verdicts.reason: Stored: 0.92. Fresh: the target's top answer is wrong on 6 of 32 variable problems and (b) reproduces it (0.81-0.84). On one fresh problem the certificate certified the stale-value answer, because M itself believes it.

verdicts.claim: CONJECTURE: a writer that hides M's best demonstration would move both score-based aggregations.
verdicts.reason: The work did not run it; I ran two. Exact hider (M's rollouts without M's top line, K=16): (b) right on 11% / 55% stored and 6% / 45% fresh, against 99% / 93%, with mean stated probability 0.73-0.82. Trained writer W5 (W3's recipe without M's rollouts in the tuning text): vote, (b) and (c) right on 9-12% / 0% (the arithmetic residue is where the planted digit is right by chance), stated probability about 1. Found score 0.01-0.12; the certificate fired on 0% (hider) and 3-12% (W5), never wrongly about the target.

verdicts.claim: Thinking helps: direct answer 10% / 24%, vote over 64 rollouts 99% / 92%; a 2.3x larger model directly 9% / 25%.
verdicts.reason: Stored: identical. Fresh: 3% / 25% against 97% / 81%. One rollout alone already gives 86% / 79%, and families and sizes were chosen on the pilot for this gap, so it is not a finding about amplification. Test problems seen in tuning: 0 of 300 (0 of 64 fresh); counting baselines 0% / 15-17%. The Qwen3-4B number was read, not re-run.

verdicts.claim: UNKNOWN: the result survives long free-form demonstrations.
verdicts.reason: Not run by the work or by me.

plain_words:
TL;DR: the numbers are right and the bin is MINOR, but the headline is narrower than it reads. The three biased writers were harmless because they still write the world model's own best line; a writer that does not moves every aggregation. No decision needed.

1. I re-ran it with my own sampler, scorer and analysis on 64 new problems (job 57920, one L40, 65 minutes, cancelled at 64 of 120 planned). Vote under the biased writer: 53% / 41%. Score-weighted: 97% / 84%, the same as the model's own rollouts. Every stored number reproduces.
2. In this pilot one line carries about 80% of the whole score, and each biased writer writes that line in a third to two thirds of its rollouts. That is why "count each demonstration once" works.
3. I tuned the same biased writer without mixing in the model's own rollouts. Vote, score-weighted and importance-weighted then all return the planted wrong answer with stated probability near 1: right 12% / 0%. Hiding only the best line: 6% / 45%.
4. The reason: both corrections normalise over what was found and throw away how much score was found. The found share (1-12% here) does flag it. A trust head that reads it, fitted on real answers with the old writers only, dropped to confidence 0.26 on the new writer (right 5%); the plain trust head stayed at 0.99. That is one calibration fit extrapolated far outside its range, so a hint.

What the work missed that you would want:
- The found share exists only because this score is a probability that sums to at most 1. A general score has no known total; what replaces it is open. You said you prefer probabilistic bounds to hard ones: the trust head reading the found share is that version.
- The regime your design is for is absent. Here the simple world model can write its own best demonstration, so search is never needed. The test needs a score the model can check but rarely write.
- Nothing was trained by the loop: no writer trained toward the score, no distillation. Items 3-4 predict that distillation would copy a writer's blind spot.
- Trust in kinds of demonstration was not built (the wrong targets are stale-value steps, which a head reading the steps could learn). Consistency across queries was not touched.
